Multiple evidence sources support the claim that scanned PDFs can weaken citation quality:

- Scanned PDFs are image-only and require OCR; without OCR, no text is extracted and citations cannot be generated [NL-006#NL-006-S03]. Even with OCR, blurry or low-quality scans can cause layout corruption, directly leading to broken citations and retrieval gaps [NL-006#NL-006-S03]. Low-resolution scanned PDFs are a recognized root cause of missing citations or broken links because the layout parser cannot determine the exact page or section ID [NL-006#NL-006-S04].

- Support and deployment data show scanned PDFs produce weak citations in practice. At one enterprise, 60% of clinical documentation is scanned image-only PDFs, and citation mapping fails for them, pointing to page one of a 200-page document or not generating a link at all—for example, a code blue checklist citation pointed to page 1 of a 150-page document instead of page 87 [NL-018#NL-018-S04]. Another account reported that 40–50% of ingested files are scanned PDFs without text layers, causing TutorChat to return answers with no source citations or with citations pointing to the entire document (e.g., page 1 of a 250-page PDF) rather than a specific section [NL-021#NL-021-S02]. Monthly audits show that the remaining citation tickets in May and June 2026 were almost entirely linked to scanned, image-only PDFs, where TutorChat struggles to establish citation anchors and often links to the start of the file [NL-011#NL-011-S05].

- Product guidance explicitly warns that ingesting a scanned or image-only PDF without OCR "may result in poor citation quality" [NL-021#NL-021-S05], and the system’s troubleshooting documentation states that questions based on low-quality scanned PDFs may lack page-specific citations due to OCR limitations [NL-028#NL-028-S03]. A proposed admin dashboard also flags scanned PDFs with low citation confidence (e.g., 45% vs. 100% for natively digital files), indicating the expected degradation [NL-021#NL-021-S05].
